messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Mark Tane grew up in a working-class family in an island community before moving to the mainland as a young adult, and at 56 he now lives alone in the wake of a divorce that has left his evenings especially quiet. He has spent much of his adult life in law enforcement and currently works as a detective, a role that suits his habit of scanning rooms and watching people closely, though he has become increasingly aware that his vigilance has long since outlived the job itself. What he first described as “just the way things were” began in childhood, when his caregiver used physical punishment in a way that was severe, unpredictable, and frightening to him. Mark remembers the house not through a neat sequence of events, but in fragments: the sensation of bracing himself, the sharpness of rage in his chest, and the sense that his mind would go blank when he tried to tell anyone exactly what had happened. Even now, when he attempts to explain those years, he loses the thread and cannot finish, as if the story breaks apart before it can reach the end.

Certain cues still carry him back with startling force. A burnt smell is one of the most potent; if something scorches in the break room at work or a pan is left too long on a stove, he can feel his body react before he has time to think. The odor does not merely remind him of the past; it can make the full memory return without warning, complete and immediate, as though he is once again in the same house and standing on the same fearful ground. He is also unsettled by people who resemble the victims from cases he has handled, particularly if they share a certain look that his mind has linked to vulnerability and injury. He notices their faces in hallways, interview rooms, and public spaces, and the sight can pull his attention sharply out of the present. He has also become wary of positive emotions in a way he finds difficult to explain to others. Moments of warmth, laughter, or ease can leave him feeling uneasy and exposed, as if a calm atmosphere is only the prelude to something going wrong.

Over the years, Mark has responded by narrowing his world. He avoids wearing clothes similar to those he associates with the time and circumstances he finds himself trying not to think about, preferring garments that feel different enough to keep him from being reminded. He detaches himself from memories when they start to surface, forcing himself away from them as soon as he senses their approach. He has also been avoiding other people more broadly, declining social invitations and keeping interactions at work efficient and brief. This has had visible consequences in his life: his divorce left him with fewer anchors outside work, and his distance from others has made it harder for him to rebuild ordinary companionship. At the office, he can function well enough in the role, but he is often alone at lunch and tends to leave quickly once the day is done.

Mark is haunted by a set of beliefs that have hardened over time. He told the therapist that what happened “proved the world doesn’t work the way people say it does,” and that his beliefs about how things are supposed to work have been completely destroyed. He also sees his own reactions with harsh self-judgment, interpreting the years after the abuse as evidence that he is a lousy coper. More painfully, he has come to believe that the event happened to him because of the sort of person he is, as though there were something in him that made him deserving of mistreatment. These beliefs sit alongside his memories rather than replacing them, and when the memories arrive they can be accompanied by intense rage. He describes a hot, immediate anger that flares when he thinks back on what was done to him, an anger that is hard to settle and that sometimes leaves him physically shaken. He also notices strong bodily reactions whenever something in the environment reminds him of the experience — his muscles tighten, his heart races, and he feels on guard before he can name why.

He has become increasingly superalert, particularly at night. Falling asleep is difficult because he feels he needs to stay alert, as if letting his guard down would invite something bad to happen. At home he checks locks, listens for noises in the building, and stays attuned to every small sound. In public and at work, that same watchfulness persists; he scans people and exits automatically, even during routine detective work. Recently, the accumulation of these experiences has worn him down enough to seek help. He said he came in because he is tired of living as though danger is always a second away, tired of losing the thread when he tries to speak about his past, and tired of feeling like he has spent a lifetime being split off from his own memories. What he fears most is that the memories will keep breaking into the present without warning, and what he hopes for, though he says it carefully, is some way to sleep without staying on guard and to move through the world without feeling as though it has been permanently shattered.
